newsitem.title: CONGO: Kabila says rebels near Zaire capital.
newsitem.headline: Kabila says rebels near Zaire capital.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Saturday said his forces, singing as they marched, were entering the Zaire capital Kinshasa from the airport about 25 km (16 miles) away.
There was no confirmation of the statement.

It came a day after Zaire's veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko left the capital for his northern jungle stronghold and it was announced that he had left his emergency-rule government in charge of national policy while keeping the title of president.
"Our troops are marching in from the airport. We are singing as we are going, and people are cheering," Kabila told Reuters by telephone from rebel-occupied Zaire.
Kabila was expected to address the nation from his Lubumbashi headquarters later on Saturday.
Bernadette Nkoye, civilian vice-governor of Kinshasa, had told Reuters earlier on Saturday the rebels were believed to be around Maluku, only 60 km (40 miles) from the city centre.

Gunfire, including two short bursts of heavy machinegun fire, could be heard not far from a Kinshasa hotel near the Zaire River shortly after a government-imposed dusk-to-dawn curfew expired on Saturday.
The significance of the gunfire was not immediately clear, and generally the city was reported calm.
Late on Friday, Mobutu's ethnic guardsmen killed Zaire's army chief, Zairean and diplomatic sources said.
They said General Mahele Lieko Bokungu, defence minister and chief of army staff, was killed at Camp Tshatshi, Mobutu's barracks residence.
A senior Western diplomat said Mahele was killed by the Special Presidential Division.
"He went to calm the guys down and then he was shot," he said.
Kabila said he had not heard of Mahele's death but termed it "very, very bad".
A diplomat, speaking to Reuters in Lusaka, said the army chief was supposed to have met Kabila in the Zambian capital on Saturday to discuss a transition of power.

"General Mahele was to meet Kabila this morning in Lusaka to discuss a handover of power. It was a deal brokered by the United States," said the clearly disappointed diplomat, who declined to be identified.
Witnesses on Friday said the head of Mobutu's presidential guard, General Nzimbi Nzale, had fled with his family across the Zaire River to Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo.
Mobutu, 66, who is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.

Kabila, 56, and his rebels took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis. They now control most of what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations, with a wealth of minerals and fertile farm land.

On Friday, Zaire's Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba said Mobutu, fighting cancer and seven months of civil war, had left Kinshasa for his northern jungle palace in Gbadolite and had stepped aside.
State television reported Mobutu had simply gone to his home region of Gbadolite on doctors' orders for "a few days of rest".
But news of Mobutu's departure triggered intense speculation that he was on his way to exile. Diplomats said later that Morocco or France were likely destinations.
Mobutu, characteristically defiant, did not resign as head of state, as demanded by Kabila and reportedly proposed by a peace plan formulated by South African President Nelson Mandela.
Kin-Kiey said Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, a key player early in Zaire's democratic transition, would negotiate with the rebels on a new transitional government and elections.
But the rebels rejected the government announcement out of hand and told Mobutu's army not to fight or loot.
Kinshasa has lived in fear that a rebel advance might trigger not a battle, but an orgy of looting by fleeing troops.
The United States welcomed the departure of Mobutu from the shattered, corruption-plagued nation but said Kabila now had to prove his democratic credentials.
"The day of the dictator should be over in Zaire and we hope that a different day has arrived," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told U.S.-based television network CNN.
Shortly before dawn there was no sign of movement by five Western military contingents in Congo, deployed in March to evacuate foreigners if necessary.
